items.s: The Long Case for Short Contracts
A contract that fits on one page is read. A contract that
fills forty pages is signed, and that difference matters
more than any clause in it. Most disputes start with a
sentence nobody remembered agreeing to, and most of
those sentences sit in the part of the document nobody
read because it looked like every other part.
The case for short contracts is not that they are simple.
It is that they force the writer to decide what matters.
When the page limit is one, a clause has to earn its
line. The payment terms stay. The three paragraphs on
notices to the registered address go, or shrink to a
sentence.
Lawyers object that the long form protects the client.
Sometimes it does. More often it protects the lawyer
from a charge of leaving something out. The two goals
are not the same, and a founder signing a partnership
paper should know which one the document serves.
There is a middle path. Write the one-page version
first, in plain words, and sign it. Attach the long form
as a reference that applies only where the short one is
silent. When the two disagree, the short one wins. The
signers then read the page that counts, and the lawyers
keep their detail.
This
works
because
people
keep
promises
they
understand. A promise written in language its maker
could not repeat from memory is a promise nobody is
in a position to keep, and a judge asked to enforce it
will start by asking what the parties thought they were
agreeing to.
None of this is new. Merchants wrote short contracts
for centuries, because the cost of a long one was a day
of a scribe's work and a week of the other side's doubt.
What changed is that copying became free, and length
became free with it. The discipline of the page limit
vanished, and nothing replaced it.
